Is Specific Performance an Argument against Libertarianism?

Posted because I think the issue is an important one. My own opinion is that contract law has been messed up for centuries and that taking the traditional framework for granted leads libertarians (and classical liberals before them) astray. For example, Walter Block and Robert Nozick argued that contractually agreed slavery should be enforceable in a libertarian society. This is indeed the position that anyone who upholds the primacy of contractual obligations must logically accept. I think it should be seen as a sufficient reductio ad absurdum of that premise.

I have a contract with a women to have sex with me for money. I pay her in advance and we meet up. Just before we are about to have sex, she has second thoughts. She says she cannot do it and gives me my money back. Can I reject the money and force her to have sex with me, because that was what the contract said?

[...]

All Libertarians I know, emphasize that we own our own bodies. [...] But if I have ownership in my own body, then I should be able to sell it like any other property.

One problem with this reasoning is that one's own body is not "like any other" alienable property. But let's change the scenario to set aside the self-ownership question and focus our attention on the matter of the nature of contractual obligation. Suppose that the woman is an artist and Nico paid her to paint a picture for him. She paints the picture but decides she wants to keep it. In the traditional common-law view, the payment constitutes a consideration that makes her promise to give up the painting enforceable (the mere promise would not be enforceable if nothing had been given in exchange). Thus a court could rule that the painting belongs to Nico.

What is the alternative? It is: that the woman has illicitly expropriated Nico's money and owes him reparations. The difference lies in which piece of property is considered to be in the wrong hads: in the traditional view, the painting; in my view, the money. Nico, after all, never had the painting - he only expected to get it in the future. This way of dealing with contract theory has considerable advantages, not the least of which is that it rules out the enforcement of rape contracts or slave contracts.

Let us say I am selling a stock to someone. We make a contract and agree on a price. After we have singed the contract he pays me and therefore the ownership of the stock changes hands. Now I have seconds thought, because the stock is now suddenly trading at a higher price. So I think I have made a bad deal. Can I now say, here is your money back, I will keep the stock?

No, because in this case, the transfers of property ownership were made simultaneously, and the contract has been fulfilled already.

US Army Motor Transport Corps convoy during its 56 day NYC to SF cross-country expedition. 1919

In 1919, the U.S. Army Motor Transport Corps deployed a convoy of military vehicles on an ambitious cross-country journey. The objectives of the trip were fourfold: encourage the construction of transcontinental highways, recruit troops for the Motor Transport Corps, demonstrate the use of military motor vehicles to the public, and evaluate the performance of different vehicles on various terrains and grades.

The convoy consisted of 81 total vehicles and nearly 300 men and officers.

After passing through Illinois, they encountered virtually no paved roads until California and even with engineers scouting and preparing the terrain ahead, the convoy logged 230 “incidents” on the trip, including stops to repair or adjust vehicles, extricate vehicles from mud, sand or ditches, and accidents and collisions.

Lieutenant Colonel Dwight D. Eisenhower, was a member of the convoy and, decades later, would make the Interstate Highway System the supreme accomplishment of his presidency.
